analysis.title: Can You Build A $2 Trillion Capex Cycle Without A Permit? JPMorgan Does The Post-Midterm Math
key_insights: JPMorgan's Lakos-Bujas says the 2026 AI buildout bottleneck has moved from chips and memory, to funding constraints, and now to regulatory risk.

JPM sees comprehensive federal AI regulation as no more likely after the midterms and a national data center moratorium as unlikely, citing the Senate's 60-vote threshold, a presidential veto, bipartisan district demand for the investment and the President's backing of the buildout.

JPM says the binding constraints have moved to the states. Newly elected Democratic governors campaigned on an immediate moratorium (Texas), pauses on new large-scale projects (Georgia, New Mexico), and conditional moratoriums requiring data centers to cover full utility costs (Ohio, Nevada).
By JPM's count, 42 of 45 local ballot measures to restrict data centers have passed or are leaning that way, nearly half in Ohio. JPM expects 'multiples' of that number on the ballot before 2028.

JPM says 2027 AI capex should be 'relatively insulated' because it funds projects already under construction and mostly funded. It has the six big spenders (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, SpaceX) at $1.7 trillion in 2027 against $1.3 trillion consensus, and says it should come in at no less than about $1.5 trillion.

JPM's hyperscaler capex path is $914 billion in 2026, $1,709 billion in 2027 and $2,030 billion in 2028. The article's own arithmetic puts that at about 87% growth in 2027 and 19% in 2028. JPM says the curve 'will likely flatten ahead of 2028 and beyond' as permitting gets harder.
JPM estimates every $100 billion of capex is worth about $9 of S&P 500 EPS, or 2.5 points of earnings growth. A $1.5 trillion 2027 figure would add 4-5% to 2027 index earnings.

Goldman's Mike Ng says capacity under construction implies 22GW and 24GW of net additions in 2027 and 2028, with Texas at 20% and 27% of those, and that the risk is 'timing rather than cancellations'. Adam Bubes raised US data center construction forecasts to $80 billion (2026) and $100 billion (2027). Jim Schneider calls 35GW of 2027 additions 'relatively low risk'.
Goldman put 45% of planned US capacity in the moratorium zone, per the article.

JPM expects near-term effects to favor assets already built or fully permitted. New development is expected to drift to friendlier states (Louisiana, North Dakota) or overseas. Tighter compute supply should give hyperscalers more pricing power, higher incremental margins and better operating cash flow.

JPM cites hyperscaler free cash flow that shrank to $77 billion over the past year. A moratorium could force a spending cut on them, which the article says helps shareholders but hurts neoclouds that have not yet built.
JPM lists workarounds for projects that still want to proceed: relocation, different materials to meet environmental rules, and alternative on-site power generation.

JPM says Texas accounts for 27% of data center capacity funded in the high-yield project finance market and calls it the key test. A slower buildout would help free cash flow, but leverage 'could still run higher' if monetization slips.
Banks shelved the junk bond sale for Anthropic's $15 billion Texas data center (Oct 29) and were left holding the bridge, per the article.
JPM credit analysts expect hyperscalers to fund 2027 without trouble absent an outside credit shock, with more of the funding mix coming from other sources, including equity.

Market reaction: in the two sessions after the election JPM's AI/data center/electrification basket fell 13.5%, after a 16.2% drop since October 1. The S&P's top 30 AI and data center names fell 7.7%.

Winners after the election were importers, child tax credit plays, low vol and healthcare. Within JPM's Blue Wave basket (ahead of the S&P by 11% since early October), hospitals rose 14.7% relative to the index in two days and Medicaid managed care 9.9%. Application software also gained, which JPM reads as a defensive corner of tech.

JPM's conclusion is that the midterms were a clearing event and data center headwinds will be 'better than feared', with moratoriums as temporary pauses rather than outright bans. Historically the S&P has been higher twelve months after every midterm since 1950, by 14.6% on average.

The article's author disagrees on 2028: an 87% then 19% capex curve was already a deceleration story, and JPM's language (flatten, delay, relocate, overseas) reads like the reason semis trade at 12x. 'Delay' looks worse from the high-yield end of the capital structure.

sector_views.rationale: JPM sees 2027 capex as insulated but expects the curve to flatten ahead of 2028 as state-level permitting tightens.
Hospitals and Medicaid managed care outperformed the index by 14.7% and 9.9% in two days after the election, within JPM's Blue Wave basket.
JPM reads its post-election gain as investors treating it as the defensive corner of tech, away from power- and construction-heavy AI infrastructure.

earnings_insights: JPM estimates every $100 billion of capex adds about $9 of S&P 500 EPS (2.5 points of earnings growth). A $1.5 trillion 2027 capex level would add 4-5% to 2027 index earnings. This is a JPM estimate, not a reported figure.

macro_indicators.indicator: Hyperscaler capex (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, SpaceX)
macro_indicators.reading: $1.7 trillion 2027 vs $1.3 trillion consensus; floor of about $1.5 trillion
macro_indicators.interpretation: JPM's 2027 estimate is well above the Street, and JPM sees it as insulated because the projects are already under construction.
Implies about 87% growth in 2027 and 19% in 2028, so the curve decelerates sharply in 2028 as permitting tightens.
Free cash flow has shrunk, so a moratorium-driven cut in spending could help it.

macro_indicators.reading: 14.6% average, higher after every midterm since 1950
macro_indicators.interpretation: JPM uses the historical record as comfort for equities after the midterms.

risk_factors: State-level moratoriums and local ballot measures delaying data center construction, especially in Texas, Georgia, Ohio and Virginia.

Texas holds 27% of data center capacity funded in the high-yield project finance market, so delays hurt borrowers whose debt service assumes a delivery date. JPM says leverage 'could still run higher' if monetization slips.
The capex curve may flatten ahead of 2028 and beyond as permitting gets harder.
Neoclouds that have not yet built face the most risk from a moratorium.
Tightening financial conditions into the December FOMC.
Mega-cap IPOs could test equity market appetite for AI paper.
vol_and_positioning: Low vol was among the winning factors in the two sessions after the election.
JPM flags the December FOMC, with financial conditions already tightening, as a date that matters for the AI capex outlook.
The article flags upcoming mega-cap IPOs as a test of how much AI paper the equity market will absorb.
geopolitical: US midterm elections: Democrats won a Congressional majority and governorships in Texas, Georgia, New Mexico, Ohio and Nevada on platforms that include data center moratoriums or pauses.
Progressive leaders in Congress have called for a national data center moratorium. The President answered by declaring data centers 'GOLD'.
Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa describes her platform as a regulatory reset ('It is not that I hate data centers'), per Goldman's desk.
cross_bank_references: Goldman's Mike Ng says the risk is 'timing rather than cancellations', matching JPM's 'delays instead of cancellations or rollbacks'.
Goldman's Giulio Esposito relays that progressive leaders in Congress called for a national moratorium and Trump answered by declaring data centers 'GOLD'.
Goldman put 45% of planned US capacity in the moratorium zone.
The article says 'virtually every other sellside desk' uses the same 'delays' framing as JPM and Goldman.

tension_points.bull_case: JPM says 2027 capex is insulated, trajectory is intact, risk is delays and not cancellations, and tighter compute supply gives hyperscalers pricing power and better cash flow. The S&P has been higher 12 months after every midterm since 1950.
tension_points.bear_case: The article argues the curve grows 87% then 19%, JPM says it will likely flatten ahead of 2028, and Texas is 27% of the high-yield funded pipeline, so delays hurt borrowers whose debt service assumes a delivery date.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Dec 10 ERCOT audit filing on the Texas interconnection queue, and the Jan 12 Texas Legislature session (regular session runs to May 31) and Jan 13 Virginia session with moratorium bills already moving.

theme_stances.key_argument: JPM says 2027 AI capex is relatively insulated and moratoriums will be temporary pauses, so the trajectory is intact.
